title: llm-d 1.0 Production-Grade Inference for Cloud-Native AI
tldr: llm-d 1.0 marks the core stack as production-ready: KV-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, KV offloading and flow control, behind a stable v1 API. IBM ran it on 500+ H100s for an internal agentic workload, and a demo shows throughput nearly doubling on the same hardware.

key_points.text: Open-weight models now close much of the gap with frontier models, so enterprises want to self-host for cost and data control.
Scaling inference is an orchestration problem: route on KV reuse and load, schedule multi-pod replicas as gangs, and manage KV state across memory tiers.
llm-d builds on Kubernetes standards: the Gateway API inference extension for the router, LeaderWorkerSet for MoE and gang scheduling, DisaggregatedSet for prefill/decode, and native KV offloading.
It now also supports batch and async APIs.
Design stays modular (use only what you need) and vendor-neutral, with more than eight accelerator types supported.
'Well-lit paths' are deployable blueprints with benchmark data: intelligent scheduling, KV cache management, flow control, and now agentic serving.
1.0 adds multi-tenant QoS (priority and fairness via flow control), router high availability, coordinated prefill/decode rollouts, session and turn affinity for agents, and a stable v1 API.

Demo: with plain round robin the KV cache hit rate is low and uneven; turning on the llm-d router raises it to about 75% and nearly doubles throughput; flow control then gives paying tiers lower latency while free users still get served.

numbers.text: A new open-weight model drops about every 11 days.
Tesla saw 3x more throughput with KV-aware routing.
Over 500 contributors and more than 25 contributing companies.
IBM: 500+ H100 GPUs serving a large MoE model with expert parallelism of 32+, peaking at 3,000 concurrent agents and about 6 million tokens a minute (6x what the workload needed).
Demo: 1,000 agents on 25 Kubernetes nodes across 40 sandboxes, about 300 requests a second.
KV cache hit rate rose from a 30-50% swing to about 75% with the llm-d router.

open_gaps.text: Going from a model recipe to a shared service (rollouts, downtime, competing teams) is still the hard part.
Tuning still takes a lot of expertise; the roadmap names operational intelligence, more automation and better guides.
Agent infrastructure (sandboxes, agent-substrate) and inference infrastructure are not yet woven together for fully self-hosted stacks.

opportunities.text: Reproduce the round robin vs llm-d router vs flow control comparison on your own cluster and publish the numbers.
Run a well-lit path on hardware or a model it has not been tested on and report how it breaks, as the speakers ask.
Case study: serving a large MoE model on previous-generation GPUs instead of paying a commercial API bill.
Read through llm-d's well-lit paths as the shortest route to a tuned deployment.
